title: Verify Lively compatibility on Windows
body:
## Desired outcome

Establish a supported way to run the existing Codex Nanoleaf map as a Lively webpage wallpaper on Windows before changing the integration. This is the first investigation in the Lively prototype.

## Scope

Use isolated synthetic map state on one selected monitor. Record the Lively version, distribution, web renderer, Windows version, and tested import/launch method. Investigate rendering, polling, selection, desktop-icon interaction, pause/resume, and server loss/recovery. The agreed prototype supports status and inspection only, with automatic startup and recovery as the eventual outcome.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: The synthetic map loads in Lively and shows the expected Lines, project colors, and task details.
- AC2: Mouse selection and inspection work with the chosen desktop-icon settings. Record any input limitations and the settings needed to reproduce the result.
- AC3: Observe polling while visible, behavior while paused or covered, and freshness after resume. Check the behavior when Lively starts before the map and when the map server disappears and returns.
- AC4: Identify and reproduce a supported URL import/launch method for one selected monitor. Record distribution-specific limitations instead of assuming that a command accepting a file path also accepts an arbitrary URL.
- AC5: Return a recommended approach for persistent addressing, page loading, and recovery, or a specific blocker with evidence and the next action. Do not weaken the existing host/origin checks, expose the server beyond loopback, or bypass the page's framing restrictions to make the trial pass.
- AC6: Record actual observations separately from documentation claims. Use synthetic state only; do not access live credentials, change live task records, or send requests to physical lights.

## Verification approach

Run the existing synthetic demo with Windows Python for the Lively trial. Use normal browser behavior as the comparison, then exercise the listed scenarios in Lively itself. Capture sanitized evidence and exact versions. Stop after recommending the integration approach or identifying a blocker; this investigation does not implement #11-#13.

Sources:
- [Lively web player](https://github.com/rocksdanister/lively/wiki/Web-Player)
- [Lively command-line controls](https://github.com/rocksdanister/lively/wiki/Command-Line-Controls)
- [Lively playback behavior](https://github.com/rocksdanister/lively/wiki/Performance)

## Dependencies

None. Windows and Lively must be available for the live trial. If Lively is absent, record that prerequisite and obtain explicit installation authorization before installing it.

## Delivery target

Windows investigation with synthetic state and a findings record on this issue. No bridge installation or physical-light verification. Any necessary repository changes require their own reviewed PR within the approved scope.

## Follow-up work

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/11 - Make the map reliable for persistent displays
- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/12 - Add an inspection-only display mode

title: Make the map reliable for persistent displays
body:
## Shared-hub ownership
Align stable identity/address discovery with [agent-device-hub#4](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/4) so Lively and future hub clients use supported discovery rather than browser-token scraping. Preserve Windows lifecycle ownership and #10; a standalone hub is not required.

## Desired outcome

Allow a persistent display to find and use the map across restarts without manually copying a new URL. The current map server selects an available port at startup, and the current map command opens a browser.

## Scope

Following #10, choose and implement a repeatable loopback address or automatic address-discovery mechanism. Add a supported way to ensure the map is running and retrieve its address without opening a browser. Keep lifecycle ownership with the Windows bridge integration. Lively-specific launch and monitor handling belong to #13.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: A caller can ensure the map is available and obtain its verified address without opening a browser window.
- AC2: Normal server restarts preserve a usable address or allow automatic discovery of the new address. The recovery contract needs no manual URL copying.
- AC3: Concurrent launch attempts produce one map server for the installation. Stale port metadata, a stopped process, and an occupied port produce defined recovery or an actionable error, never attachment to an unrelated service.
- AC4: Preserve loopback-only binding, exact Host validation, origin/token requirements for editing routes, and the exclusion of Nanoleaf credentials from responses.
- AC5: Existing tray map opening and editing still work. Restart and recovery preserve task records, reservations, project preferences, modes, scene choices, unread tracking, and animation timing.
- AC6: Document the selected address/lifecycle contract and its failure behavior in the issue-linked design and affected capability specification. Preserve other installations, worktrees, and process owners.

## Verification approach

Add focused isolated lifecycle and HTTP tests for startup, concurrent starts, stale metadata, restart, and port collision. Run python3 scripts/check.py, npm run test:browser, and the workflow checks after npm ci when OpenSpec changes are made. Exercise relevant Windows process behavior with isolated state.

Deliver through an isolated worktree and reviewed PR. Use an issue-linked OpenSpec change for changed behavior, focused red/green checks, independent Standards and Specification reviews, every configured CI job, and main CI readback. UI changes require explicit human approval of the current candidate before merge. Keep revision-specific evidence in the PR.

## Dependencies

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/10 - Verify Lively compatibility on Windows

Blocked until #10 establishes the supported addressing and loading approach.

Additional shared prerequisites:
- [agent-device-hub#4](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/4)

## Delivery target

Source-only. Installed startup and recovery are accepted through #14 after #13 is complete. This issue does not authorize an installed bridge upgrade.

## Follow-up work

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/13 - Integrate Lively startup and recovery

title: Add an inspection-only display mode
body:
## Desired outcome

Provide a display view suitable for a Lively prototype that shows current status and lets the user inspect Lines and tasks without editing bridge settings.

## Scope

Reuse the current map geometry, physical Line numbering, project colors, task associations, and inspector information. Provide a display entry point served by the existing local map server. Keep the current map's editing interface available. This issue delivers the functional inspection view. Real-time rendering is defined separately in #17 and may later be reused here; it is not a prerequisite for this prototype. The ambient visual redesign remains deferred in #16.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: The display shows the same current Line identities, status colors, projects, task placement, and waiting tasks as the normal map.
- AC2: Clicking a Line or task selects it and exposes the relevant details. Refresh preserves valid selection and handles a selected task disappearing.
- AC3: The display exposes no assignment, project-color editing, status-palette editing, animation or celebration selection, mode, half-swap, project-override, Locate, or physical-preview actions and sends no mutation requests. Selection does not mark tasks read or trigger Locate.
- AC4: Failed polling visibly identifies stale or disconnected data rather than presenting it as current. Reconnection and resume refresh the view without a manual reload once the page is running.
- AC5: Task titles remain text, and the display receives no Nanoleaf credential. The normal map's protected editing routes retain their existing checks.
- AC6: The page works in the Lively renderer validated by #10 and in a normal browser on the selected monitor. Connection and inspection controls remain usable at the tested display scale.
- AC7: Preserve existing state allocation and lighting behavior. Display-only preferences, if introduced, must not alter the user's saved lighting settings or depend on Lively retaining browser cookies.

## Verification approach

Use synthetic browser scenarios for status agreement, selection retention, disappearing tasks, reconnection, stale-data indication, title escaping, and the absence of mutation requests. Run python3 scripts/check.py, npm run test:browser, and the required workflow checks after npm ci. Record the human UI review against the current candidate.

Deliver through an isolated worktree and reviewed PR. Use an issue-linked OpenSpec change for changed behavior, focused red/green checks, independent Standards and Specification reviews, every configured CI job, and main CI readback. UI changes require explicit human approval of the current candidate before merge. Keep revision-specific evidence in the PR.

## Dependencies

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/10 - Verify Lively compatibility on Windows

Blocked until #10 confirms rendering and input compatibility. #11 can proceed independently after #10; integration of both is #13.

## Delivery target

Source-only. Live Lively acceptance belongs to #14. No bridge installation or physical-light changes.

## Follow-up work

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/13 - Integrate Lively startup and recovery

## Related work

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/17 - Show bridge-controlled lights live in the app

Configuration and physical-preview controls from #18, #19, and #20 belong in the regular app. They do not change this inspection-only boundary.

title: Integrate Lively startup and recovery
body:
## Desired outcome

Once configured, the inspection display returns on one selected monitor at Windows sign-in and after bridge or Lively restarts without copying a new URL.

## Scope

Implement the Windows integration using #10's supported Lively method, #11's map lifecycle/address contract, and #12's inspection view. Include readiness checks, launch/reload handling, monitor selection, opt-in startup configuration, and a setup/disable/removal runbook. Keep presentation and bridge state ownership in the existing components.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: Setup detects the supported Lively installation and reports missing prerequisites clearly. It configures one selected monitor using the inspection view.
- AC2: Automatic startup ensures the map is available before loading the display. If Lively starts first and its initial page load fails, recovery still succeeds when the map becomes available.
- AC3: The integration recovers from map restart, Lively restart, and sleep/resume without URL copying. Retries are bounded or use backoff and expose actionable persistent failures.
- AC4: Repeated setup or launch does not duplicate startup entries, wallpaper entries, or map servers.
- AC5: Disabling/removing the integration removes only its owned configuration and processes, with documented steps for restoring the prior wallpaper on the selected monitor. Other monitors and wallpapers remain under user control.
- AC6: Explicit disabling or selecting a different wallpaper is respected. Recovery must not continuously reclaim the monitor from the user.
- AC7: All bridge coordination runs through Windows Python. No new light writer, direct Codex database access, or credential delivery to Lively is introduced.
- AC8: Document supported versions/distributions, installation and upgrade procedure, recovery, ownership, and removal. Any bridge upgrade must use bridge/install-modes.ps1 and preserve live state.

## Verification approach

Use isolated Windows process/command fixtures for readiness, startup order, retries, duplicate prevention, and cleanup ownership. Exercise the supported Lively launch method with synthetic state. Run the Python, browser, and applicable workflow checks; validate PowerShell changes in Windows PowerShell. #14 supplies the full installed acceptance matrix.

Deliver through an isolated worktree and reviewed PR. Use an issue-linked OpenSpec change for changed behavior, focused red/green checks, independent Standards and Specification reviews, every configured CI job, and main CI readback. UI changes require explicit human approval of the current candidate before merge. Keep revision-specific evidence in the PR.

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/12 - Add an inspection-only display mode

Blocked until both source prerequisites are complete. Their designs must incorporate #10's compatibility findings.

## Delivery target

## Follow-up work

title: Run and evaluate the installed Lively prototype
body:
## Desired outcome

Demonstrate that the completed Lively prototype is reliable and useful during actual work, then decide whether to proceed with an ambient view.

## Scope

Perform an explicitly authorized Windows installation/configuration and acceptance trial on one selected monitor. Start with synthetic state, then observe live tasks through the existing bridge. Record visibility, distraction, resource use, startup/recovery behavior, and the user's assessment.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: Record the tested source revision, Windows and Lively versions/distribution/renderer, selected monitor, installation owner, backup, and rollback steps before changing the installed integration.
- AC2: Synthetic scenarios establish working, question, blocked, unread, waiting, and idle display behavior before the live-task trial. Status and Line/task associations agree with the normal map.
- AC3: The installed display supports inspection and issues no editing or Locate requests. Existing task records, unread state, assignments, saved preferences, modes, scene choices, and the single light writer are preserved.
- AC4: Verify Windows sign-in, Lively-before-map startup, map restart, Lively restart, sleep/resume, and pause/resume. The chosen monitor returns to current status without manual URL repair.
- AC5: Exercise repeat setup and disable/removal. Confirm that unrelated wallpapers/monitors and bridge state are preserved and record the restoration result.
- AC6: Measure CPU, GPU, and memory with the display visible and paused during a normal work session. Record duration, resolution, sampling method, and baseline so the results can guide an ambient rendering budget.
- AC7: Obtain the user's assessment of readability, usefulness, and distraction. Record a decision to keep the prototype, revise it, or proceed to ambient planning, with identified limitations and follow-up work.

## Verification approach

Run the full Windows acceptance matrix and record actual observations, sanitized screenshots where useful, resource measurements, and the user's decision. Distinguish automated source checks, installed software behavior, and any separately authorized physical-light observations. Do not create or clear real task records merely to manufacture test states.

Use bridge/install-modes.ps1 for any authorized upgrade of an existing bridge, with its backup and preservation procedure. Do not use fresh setup for an upgrade. Keep this issue open if any required installed acceptance remains incomplete.

Blocked until #13 and its prerequisite source work are complete. Before the trial, obtain explicit installation/configuration authorization and identify the installation owner.

title: Expose authoritative light rendering state for display clients
body:
## Ownership

The fresh Linux installation's existing worker owns light writes and the timeline it sends. This issue exposes a read-only snapshot of that worker output. The wall map's live renderer and physical parity belong to [#17](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/17); this issue does not change current wall-map animation. Legacy Windows installations keep their existing path; adding Windows-specific behavior is outside scope.

Reuse relevant fields from [agent-device-hub#4](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/4) where useful. The shared overview and basic controls do not wait for this work.

## Desired outcome

Provide display clients with enough last-sent rendering data to reproduce bridge-controlled output without inferring it from task status or scheduling effects themselves.

## Scope

Add a read-only `GET /api/rendering` route to the existing loopback wall-map server for the current Linux-owned Lines worker. Read directly from private state without refreshing metadata, acquiring device geometry, contacting the controller, or starting a worker. Include physical zone identity, encoded colors and frame durations, loop/effect phase, effective brightness and a compact outcome: pending, last successfully sent, failed/partial, or externally controlled/unknown.

Retain only the latest output receipt needed to describe the current worker output; do not add output history, subscriptions, replay queues, a new listener/authentication system, or a second writer. Preserve existing task/effect epochs and the current palette, one outward pulse with its two-second cycle, completion comet defaults, split project/status halves, and Work/Quiet/Free behavior. Future palettes and effects remain with #18-#20.

A successful HTTP command means the device accepted the command; it does not prove what the lights visibly produced. Scenes or streams whose frames are unavailable remain externally controlled/unknown. A simulated on-screen preview is not live worker output.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: A rendering read provides the worker's last successfully accepted encoded frames, physical zone identity, frame durations, looping/phase and brightness needed by a display client to reproduce bridge-controlled output.
- AC2: The response distinguishes pending work, last successful output, failed or partially accepted updates, and external/unknown output. It does not describe command acceptance as optical confirmation.
- AC3: Reads do not refresh task metadata, advance effects, reserve sources, clear unread state, change assignments/preferences, acquire device geometry, contact the controller, start a worker, or write lights. Reads and reconnects do not replay expired effects.
- AC4: The latest output receipt and timing remain available after worker or map-server restart without resetting task, scene or project preferences. Existing installations acquire receipt storage without destructive migration.
- AC5: The endpoint reads through the existing loopback server and retains its Host and no-store protections. It contains no Nanoleaf credentials. Current wall-map rendering remains unchanged; #17 consumes this data.

## Verification

Use the fake controller, isolated database and fake clock to compare representative worker payloads for a two-second pulse and completion comet. Check pending and failed/partial outcomes, repeated reads, restart recovery, and that the GET-only rendering endpoint rejects writes without changing the last-sent worker receipt. The renderer-specific check that an on-screen-only preview stays separate from live worker output belongs to #17.

For implementation, run `python3 scripts/check.py`. The wall map itself is unchanged, so browser rendering checks belong with #17. Physical comparison and installation remain separate, explicitly authorized work under #17/#55.

## Dependencies

None. The shared envelope in agent-device-hub#4 is available for alignment; it does not block this work. The ambient-view decision and Lively prototype do not gate it.

## Follow-up work

- [#17](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/17) - Render bridge-controlled lights live and verify physical parity.
- [#18](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/18) - Configure project and status colors.
- [#19](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/19) - Choose and preview completion celebrations.
- [#20](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/20) - Customize animation for each status.
- [#16](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/16) - Build the deferred ambient view.
- [#21](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/21) - Investigate mirroring externally controlled Nanoleaf scenes.

title: Build the ambient view
body:
## Desired outcome

If selected after the Lively prototype, provide a spacious ambient wall visualization that communicates task status and offers details on demand.

## Scope

Deferred ambient work. Reuse the Lively integration and the live renderer from #17, supporting fullscreen browser use. Consume the effective palettes from #18, celebration choices from #19, and per-status animations from #20 through #15's shared output contract. Add an uncluttered wall presentation, on-demand inspection, and reduced-motion support. Settle idle and Work/Quiet/Free presentation and the performance budget using the prototype findings before implementation.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: An approved design defines idle, Work, Quiet, and Free presentation, inspection, and reduced-motion behavior. Do not imply that the display mirrors arbitrary Nanoleaf scenes unless a separate capability supports that claim.
- AC2: Physical Line numbering, project/task associations, status meaning, and waiting-task visibility remain consistent with the normal map.
- AC3: Reuse #17's renderer and #15's output/timing contract with the user's effective palettes, celebration choices, and status-animation settings. Reconnection and resume do not replay expired effects. Blocked and question alerts retain their semantic priority and remain recognizable regardless of selected hues. Any reduced-motion presentation is explicit rather than being presented as an exact animated live mirror.
- AC4: Details are available on demand without exposing assignment, palette, animation, celebration, mode, Locate, or physical-preview controls. Configuration remains in the regular app. Selection does not change bridge state or mark tasks read.
- AC5: The view works in the verified Lively configuration and a fullscreen browser at the tested display size. Reduced-motion behavior and text/indicator contrast are reviewed with the user.

- AC7: The user approves the current UI candidate before merge. Record source, installed display, and any physical-light evidence separately.

Use deterministic timing and browser scenarios for status semantics, overlapping animation, expired effects, recovery, inspection, and reduced motion. Compare actual Windows resource measurements and readability with the prototype. Run the canonical Python, browser, and applicable workflow checks.

Deliver through an isolated worktree and reviewed PR. title: Show bridge-controlled lights live in the app
body:
## Shared-hub ownership
Keep the reusable Nanoleaf visual renderer here. Future hub previews may consume this timeline after parity verification; [agent-device-hub#6](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/6)'s overview does not depend on it. Do not add a device writer or status interpreter.

## Desired outcome

Make the regular app's wall visualization track bridge-controlled physical lights in real time, including animation rather than only one-second status-color updates.

## Scope

Consume #15's rendering contract in a reusable visual renderer for the current map. Match task pulses and waves, per-project halves, completion effects, Locate, and physical previews. Make the renderer reusable by the inspection-only wallpaper and future ambient view without requiring either deliverable to finish first.

Keep on-screen effect demonstrations visibly separate from the live wall visualization. External Nanoleaf scenes are a separate investigation.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: For bridge-controlled output, the correct physical zones show the same encoded colors, relative brightness, frame transitions, looping, and timing as the worker output. Project/status halves and physical Line numbering remain correct after rotation and flips.
- AC2: Verify a maximum visual phase difference of 250 ms in the agreed visible-app acceptance scenarios on the user's PC. Record actual measurements and the measurement method. This measures UI-versus-wall alignment, not the separate delay before a task-status event reaches the worker. A failure to meet the target remains an acceptance gap unless the user explicitly revises it.
- AC3: Rendering follows successfully sent output and exposes pending, failed/uncertain, stale, and externally controlled states. Do not present requested-but-unsent settings or arbitrary scene guesses as current physical output.
- AC4: Pause/resume, browser backgrounding, reconnect, server restart, and task interruption recover to current output without replaying expired waves or celebrations.
- AC5: Selecting Lines/tasks and observing the live view do not mutate task state, mark tasks read, start animations, or send light writes. Existing editing actions remain explicit in the regular map; the wallpaper remains inspection-only.
- AC6: An on-screen preview is labeled and separate from live output. A physical preview appears in the live view while the worker plays it, and normal current output returns afterward.
- AC7: Physical comparison covers Work and Quiet, overlapping blocked/question alerts, split halves, an existing completion comet, and Locate. Extend frame-parity and device scenarios when the linked new palettes and effects become available. Free and idle external scenes display their known control state without claiming unverified per-zone mirroring.
- AC8: Preserve keyboard focus and selection during updates, and record CPU/GPU/memory behavior while visible and paused. No second animation scheduler or light writer is introduced.

## Verification approach

Use deterministic frame/timing browser scenarios against #15, including failed/partial sends and restart/no-replay cases. Compare the visible UI with physical output using synchronized recording or another reproducible observation method with sufficient timing resolution. Include representative animation transitions and report observed maximum skew. Matching software frames alone does not establish physical synchronization.

title: Configure project and status colors consistently
body:
## Shared-hub ownership
Use shared semantic identifiers from [agent-device-hub#2](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/issues/2) with an explicit mapping for current working/question/blocked/unread behavior. Palettes/brightness stay device presentation preferences. Priority cannot derive from RGB; clients consume effective colors.

## Desired outcome

Let the user choose project and alert/status colors while keeping physical output, the live map, previews, and legends consistent.

## Scope

Retain the existing per-project color pickers and saved values. Add a global configurable palette for working, question, blocked, and unread states in the regular app. Reuse the shared rendering contract and live view. Per-project status palettes and new status categories are outside this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: Existing project color selection continues to work. Add separately labeled color choices for working, question, blocked, and unread statuses.
- AC2: The effective palette is consistent across physical output, both Line halves where applicable, the live map, effect previews, and legends. The browser no longer relies on a separate fixed status-color table.
- AC3: Blocked and question precedence derives from status, not RGB values. Changing blocked to purple, for example, retains the same alert priority. Labels and other status identification remain usable independently of color choice.
- AC4: Save palettes across restarts and upgrades. Existing installations retain their project colors and current status defaults until explicitly changed.
- AC5: Provide clearly scoped resets so resetting status colors does not erase project colors or unrelated settings. Validate input and reject invalid colors without partially applying a palette.
- AC6: Applying or resetting colors updates current output without restarting status epochs, replaying initial waves or completed celebrations, or changing task/Line assignments.
- AC7: Expose pending and failed updates consistently with #15. Preserve Work/Quiet/Free behavior, saved scenes, and existing animation-coverage settings.
- AC8: Color editing remains in the regular app. The inspection-only wallpaper receives effective colors but exposes no editing or physical-preview action.

## Verification approach

Add isolated persistence/migration tests and exact frame comparisons for custom colors, including arbitrary hues for high-priority statuses. Exercise normal-map editing, reset scope, invalid input, legends, preview/live agreement, and no-replay behavior in browser tests. Record software evidence separately from physical color/brightness observations.

Run python3 scripts/check.py after Python changes, npm run test:browser after map/API changes, and npm run check:workflow plus npm run test:workflow after npm ci for OpenSpec/workflow changes. Validate PowerShell changes in Windows PowerShell.

Deliver source changes through an isolated worktree and reviewed PR, using an issue-linked OpenSpec change for changed behavior. Use focused red/green checks, independent Standards and Specification reviews, all configured CI jobs, and main CI readback. UI changes require explicit human approval of the current candidate before merge. Keep revision-specific evidence in the PR.

title: Check feasibility of mirroring externally controlled Nanoleaf scenes
body:
## Desired outcome

Decide whether externally controlled Nanoleaf output can be observed well enough to justify a later live mirror. If it cannot, the app should show an honest externally controlled/unknown state.

## Scope

Review authoritative API documentation first. Consider three output groups: solid colors and static saved scenes; animated or randomized saved scenes; and externally driven output such as music and Screen Mirror. Distinguish current per-zone output and animation phase from a scene name, palette, effect definition, or global setting. This investigation does not block the bridge-controlled live view in #17.

## Acceptance criteria

- AC1: Identify documented read-only observation methods for each output group. State whether they expose current per-zone colors and brightness, animation phase, only metadata, or nothing relevant. Cite the evidence and its limits. A scene definition or palette alone is not proof of current physical output.
- AC2: Summarize each group as observable, partly observable, or unknown, and recommend whether live mirroring is worth pursuing. If documentation shows no plausible way to observe current per-zone output and phase for a group, stop there and recommend an externally controlled/unknown UI state for it. An undocumented method is not proof that observation is impossible.
- AC3: If a plausible read-only method exists, define one small follow-up device trial to verify it. Measure timing and controller impact only in that later trial if actual frame data is available; #17's 250 ms target applies to bridge-controlled output and is not an acceptance target for this documentation review.
- AC4: Preserve Free mode's no-polling-after-handoff behavior. This issue adds no polling, light control, stream, competing writer, scene emulation, or credentials in the browser. Any device trial or change to Free-mode observation needs its own authorized scope and an identified device owner.

## Verification approach

Start with the [official Nanoleaf API documentation](https://nanoleaf.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/nlapid/pages/2789310530/Nanoleaf+Light+Panels+Open+API+Documentation) and its [documentation index](https://support.nanoleaf.me/hc/en-us/articles/46020382680468-API-Nanoleaf-OpenAPI-Documentation-Forum-Guidelines). Record the relevant methods and what their responses actually establish. Do not treat an effect listing, a successful HTTP response, or a documented write stream as current-frame telemetry.

## Dependencies

None. Coordinate terminology with #15's rendering/freshness model and #17's externally controlled state. No Lively or ambient work is required.

## Delivery target

A brief evidence table and a recommendation for each output group. Stop at findings and, only where warranted, one bounded follow-up trial proposal. No source changes, installation, controller exercises, or physical-light acceptance are part of this issue.

- https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/15 - Expose authoritative light rendering state for display clients

Line numbers fit the Prism crystal style and remain easy to identify and select without overlapping neighbouring Lines. Show neutral luminous numerals for selected, highlighted, hovered, and keyboard-focused Lines, with an optional show-all control.

## Scope

Refine this existing number-clearance issue as part of the approved Prism work. Keep its unresolved compact-layout regression and stable-identity requirements. Do not create a duplicate numbering issue.

Original reproduction from the #22 review in PR #24: at 90 or 270 degrees in 800×844 and 390×844 layouts, tags 6, 7, 10, and 11 sit within or close to a neighbouring Line's track. The earlier tags cleared their own selection ring but used the side away from the wall center. Keep neighbour clearance as the placement goal when replacing pill tags with luminous numerals. Use the final crystal body and selection bounds rather than assuming the old 10-unit track or 12-unit selected half-width is still correct.

The default visibility follows selected/highlighted/hovered/focused Lines. Multiple selected Lines can show their numbers at once. Show-all is a browser-local display preference, off by default; it never changes physical lights or bridge allocation. Preserve the inspector, task/project associations, pending selection state, multi-selection modifiers, and explicit Locate action. Exclude physical renumbering, a general layout editor, tray work, and service migration.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1: At 1440, 800, and 390 px, every supported map rotation and flip has no numeral/label bounds intersecting a neighbouring Line's final crystal track or active selection bounds. Labels remain inside the canvas. Cover the original compact-layout regression, the show-all state, and multiple simultaneously selected/highlighted labels. Preserve the existing all-rotations overlap guard and adapt it to the final material geometry.

Idle unselected/unhighlighted/unhovered/unfocused Lines hide their numbers; show-all reveals every number. Touch selection can reveal and retain a number without requiring hover.

Accessible names retain stable Line numbers even when decorative numerals are hidden.

Shared-input cutover and rollback remain separate from the fresh Linux installation and do not import Windows runtime state into Linux.

The [hub architecture](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#ownership) keeps provider/session interpretation in the shared core and device presentation in Nanoleaf. title: Introduce device-aware Nanoleaf state and geometry contracts
body:
## Desired outcome

Let the Linux bridge state describe more than one Nanoleaf device without duplicating task ingestion or losing the existing Lines configuration. Establish the storage and geometry shape that the worker, renderers, and interfaces in [#42](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/42) and [#43](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/43) build on.

This is a personal project with one operator and one Linux installation. The issue is sized for that. It asks for a Linux-only schema change, a small device registry, and one migration test. It leaves out Windows compatibility, adapter layers, and a future allocation pool.

## Scope

A device is one physical Nanoleaf controller with its attached lights. An element is one physical Line or triangle. A zone is an independently controlled lighting part: a Line has two, a triangle has one. Each device owns its own placement and capacity; there is no separate pool concept in this version.

Shared data stays shared: task history, task IDs, project identity, task-project overrides, status epochs, and Codex unread evidence keep one owner. Device-scoped data gains a device column: slot assignments, project reservations, waiting state, modes, pending map edits, completion-effect state, and saved scenes.

Follow [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md) and the [Linux installation guide](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/linux-install.md). Runtime and private state live under `~/.local/share/codex-nanoleaf`. The existing worker remains the sole light writer.

Out of scope here:

- The legacy Windows installation. It keeps its current schema and is not migrated, adapted, or opened. No Windows fixtures or Windows-owned coordination.
- A compatibility adapter layer. Existing functions gain a device argument that defaults to the original Lines device.
- A pool identity separate from device identity. [#47](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/47) is deferred; a column can be added when it matters.
- Enabling personal hardware, reading NL22 layout, or rendering on Panels. [#42](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/42) owns runtime integration and [#43](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/43) owns NL22 geometry and effect payloads.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1: Task ingestion, task IDs, project identity, task-project overrides, status epochs, and Codex unread evidence keep one shared owner. Device-scoped rows reference that shared data rather than copying the task reducer.
- [ ] AC2: A device registry records id, kind (`lines` or `panels`), address, and token reference. Device identity survives a configured address change. Element identity is device-qualified, so equal panel IDs on two devices cannot collide. The original Lines device keeps the identity established by #28.
- [ ] AC3: Slot assignments, waits, comets, line preferences, display state, map settings, pending edits, locate, mode, and saved scene are keyed by device. Uniqueness becomes device plus slot, so one task can hold one placement on Lines and one on Panels.
- [ ] AC4: The layout file holds one entry per device. Each element carries its physical ID, its existing numbering, and a zone list: two for a Line, one for a triangle. Task assignment and map presentation read that shape rather than the Lines-only pairing. Initialization rejects a malformed layout and keeps the last valid one.
- [ ] AC5: Migration runs inside the existing Linux initialization as guarded column additions with default `lines`, and is idempotent. One fixture test opens a copy of a pre-change Linux database, runs initialization twice, and checks that tasks, project and half preferences, scene choice and brightness, an active comet, pending edits, and protected-API credentials and request history survive with their values and epochs intact.
- [ ] AC6: Callers with no device target continue to address the original Lines device. Existing Lines-only behavior, the Python suite, and browser checks pass unchanged apart from the new device parameter.
- [ ] AC7: A short ADR at the next unused number records device identity, device-scoped state, the Linux-only migration, and the deliberate omission of Windows support, adapters, and pools. Behavioral requirements go in the applicable specs with their guide links updated.

## Verification approach

Use one isolated Linux database fixture containing active tasks, unread completions, an active comet, pending edits, a saved scene, and protected-API history. Compare preserved values and epochs before and after migration and repeated initialization. Exercise equal panel IDs across two registry entries and an address change with fake addresses and no credentials. Run the full Python suite and the OpenSpec and workflow checks; run browser checks if the map's API changes. These checks use temporary state and fake transport.

## Dependencies

- #28 is satisfied: the protected controller API was delivered through PR #39, merged as 3c2911c3bdd32f69c39883a0253e78858afc19df. Refresh that baseline before implementation.
- Linux source support was delivered by [#54](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/54) through [PR #57](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/pull/57). [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md) is the runtime ownership baseline.
- Next: [#42](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/42).

## Delivery target

Source-only foundation on the Linux runtime. The installation and physical trial with both Lines and Panels remain with [#46](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/46), whose Windows-specific criteria need reconciliation with ADR 0007 before that trial. This issue does not install or upgrade a personal runtime, change hooks or services, or operate lights.

## Planning and delivery

Source delivery follows AGENTS.md and docs/sdlc.md: an isolated issue branch, issue-linked OpenSpec planning, focused red/green checks, independent Standards and Specification reviews against the same committed comparison, required CI, guarded merge, and main-CI readback. UI changes require human approval of the current candidate.

The issue-linked planning root is `openspec/changes/gh-41-device-state-geometry/`. Check active and archived changes for this exact issue before creating or reusing it.

## Revision note

Scope reduced on 2026-09-22 for a single-operator Linux installation. The original body required legacy Windows migration and coordination, source compatibility adapters, a pool identity separate from device identity, and a fresh-versus-migrated verification matrix. I removed those. The edit history holds the prior text.

title: Run independent Lines and Light Panels projections in the Nanoleaf runtime
body:
## Desired outcome

Let the existing Python worker display the same eligible task activity on Lines and Light Panels while keeping placement, modes, effects, scenes, and failures independent for each device.

This is a personal project with one operator and one Linux installation. The issue is sized for that. It builds on the device registry and device-scoped state from [#41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41) and leaves out Windows compatibility, adapter layers, and a combined allocation pool.

## Scope

Consume the device registry, device-scoped tables, and layout shape from [#41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41). Integrate mirrored allocation, device-specific output scheduling, existing scene restoration, explicit CLI targeting, and multi-device use of the protected API delivered by #28. Use the existing Lines renderer and a fake second renderer here; [#43](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/43) supplies the real NL22 adapter.

Keep one ingestion path and the existing Python worker as the sole light writer. Follow [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md): hooks, CLI, wall map, controller, and worker coordinate through private Linux SQLite, and local MCP uses direct loopback HTTP.

The [hub architecture](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/blob/main/docs/architecture.md#ownership) assigns provider/session interpretation to the shared core and device projections to Nanoleaf. Keep allocation, effects, modes, scene restoration, and output scheduling in Nanoleaf. [#29](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/29) owns shared-feed input; do not duplicate the shared reducer.

Out of scope here:

- The legacy Windows installation. It is not migrated, adapted, or tested. No Windows fixtures or forwarding coverage.
- A compatibility adapter layer. Callers with no device target address the original Lines device through the default device argument from #41.
- A combined allocation pool. [#47](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/47) is deferred.
- Shared monitoring migration, new MCP infrastructure, and new generic scene, brightness, power, zone, or preview commands.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1: A working task can occupy one element on each device. Each device independently preserves valid assignments, project reservations, Shared overflow, capacity, and its waiting list. A full or failed device does not redistribute tasks to the other device.
- [ ] AC2: Completion/read evidence is shared, while completion queues, active source reservations, and pending display edits are device-scoped. Reading a completed task through existing Codex evidence clears its indications on both devices; the map/API never marks it read.
- [ ] AC3: Each device independently persists Work, Quiet, and Free and restores its own latest saved scene and brightness. A change affecting one device does not clear the other device's effects, pending edits, mode, or restoration state. Free makes no further device requests after successful handoff.
- [ ] AC4: Preserve two-second status epochs, the one outward pulse, red/yellow priority, and one completion comet per eligible completion per device. Entering Work, registering a device, and recovering a connection do not reset epochs or replay obsolete effects. New task-project overrides preserve affected active comet sources until their existing completion boundary.
- [ ] AC5: Catch failures and schedule bounded retries per device. A failing device cannot abort the other device's due updates or overwrite its last successful outcome. Preserve #28's hold on failed/uncertain machine requests: automatic retry must not replay them; a fresh explicit request is required.
- [ ] AC6: Add explicit device targeting to CLI mode/status controls. Existing commands with no target still address the original Lines device, regardless of registry order. An explicit Both devices operation makes two targeted requests and returns both outcomes, including partial success; it does not promise atomic physical effects.
- [ ] AC7: Protected discovery, snapshots, commands, revisions, request replay, feeds, and credential permissions distinguish devices. Preserve the existing Lines identity and existing credentials' target scope; registering a second device never silently broadens access. A request, replay, or revocation for one target cannot execute against the other.
- [ ] AC8: Retain the adopted shared wire contract and its mode-only capability scope. Compose Both devices from individually targeted operations rather than adding a bulk command to the shared schema. Keep authentication, origin/Host checks, time/queue bounds, and private destination registration.
- [ ] AC9: Snapshot/feed and cached display reads do not discover device geometry, allocate tasks, advance effects, send lights, or refresh device evidence by observation alone. The worker retains these responsibilities.

## Verification approach

Use fake clocks, isolated Linux task state, two fake devices, and a fake launcher. Cover mirroring, per-device overflow and reservations, mixed modes, source-preserving deferred edits, completion/read handling, outage/reconnect, partial Both devices outcomes, and no-replay across restart. Exercise equal request counters on different targets, stale commands, target-scoped permissions and discovery, revocation, and repeated reads. Run the Python suite, protected contract fixtures, browser checks for API changes, and OpenSpec/workflow checks. These source checks require no live installation.

## Dependencies

- Blocked by [#41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41). Begin only after its registry and device-scoped state are delivered.
- Next: [#43](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/43). Coordinate compatibility with #29 and #33; neither is a prerequisite for this automatic task display path.

## Delivery target

Source-only runtime and interface integration on the Linux runtime. No personal configuration, hardware enrollment, installation, or physical-light operations. [#46](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/46) owns the later installed and physical trial with both Lines and Panels; reconcile its Windows-specific criteria with [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md) before that trial.

## Planning and delivery

Source delivery follows AGENTS.md and docs/sdlc.md: an isolated issue branch, issue-linked OpenSpec planning, focused red/green checks, independent Standards and Specification reviews against the same committed comparison, required CI, guarded merge, and main-CI readback. UI changes require human approval of the current candidate.

The next authorized delivery or guide coordinator owns refreshing the affected Nanoleaf backlog inputs and narrative in a linked hub PR under the [shared guide procedure](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/agent-device-hub/blob/main/docs/work-guide/README.md), followed by separately authorized publication and live verification.

Let the existing Python worker display the same task activity on Lines and original triangular NL22 Light Panels. Each triangle shows one task with the bridge's colors and animations, and each device keeps its own placement, mode, effects, saved scene and failures.

This is a personal project with one operator and one Linux installation. The issue is sized for that. It absorbs the device-worker scope from [#42](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/42), which is closed in favor of this issue.

## Scope

Build on the device registry, device-scoped tables and layout shape delivered by [#41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41) in PR #65. The work has two parts:

1. **Device worker.** Mirrored per-device allocation, device-specific output scheduling, per-device mode and scene restoration, per-device failure isolation and explicit CLI targeting.
2. **NL22 renderer.** NL22 geometry interpretation and a payload renderer alongside the existing split-zone Lines renderer. Reuse HTTP custom-effect timelines instead of adding a streaming writer.

Keep one ingestion path, including the shared-input path from [#29](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/29), and keep the existing Python worker as the only light writer. Follow [ADR 0007](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007-linux-runtime-ownership.md): hooks, CLI, wall map, controller and worker coordinate through private Linux SQLite, and local MCP uses direct loopback HTTP. Allocation, effects, modes, scene restoration and output scheduling stay in Nanoleaf; do not duplicate the shared reducer.

Close the known gaps [ADR 0009](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/decisions/0009-device-aware-state.md) assigned to #42, and update that ADR's gap paragraph to point here:

- The worker renders and applies mode changes for the original device only.
- Display-cache clears, `setup --reset` and shared-source switching clear every device.

The target reported by the user is model NL22, firmware 5.2.2, hardware 1.6.2. The supplied photo shows 18 triangles in three connected hexagons, with the center hexagon raised. Treat that as the expected arrangement, not verified panel identities. [#46](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/46) checks device-reported model, layout and physical orientation. Keep the configured address and original photo out of GitHub issue attachments and repository fixtures.

Out of scope here:

- A second device on the protected controller API, integration settings API or local MCP. Those keep addressing the original Lines device. Open a new issue if the hub UI later needs Panels over the API.
- A "Both devices" CLI operation. Run the targeted command once per device.
- The legacy Windows installation, its fixtures and its regression coverage.
- A compatibility adapter layer. Callers with no device target address the original Lines device through #41's default device argument.
- A combined allocation pool. [#47](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/47) is deferred.
- Shared monitoring migration and new MCP infrastructure.

## Acceptance criteria

### Device worker

- [ ] AC1: A working task can occupy one element on each device. Each device independently keeps valid assignments, project reservations, Shared overflow, capacity and its waiting list. A full or failed device does not redistribute tasks to the other device.
- [ ] AC2: Completion and read evidence is shared; completion queues, active source reservations and pending display edits are device-scoped. Reading a completed task through existing Codex evidence clears its indications on both devices. The map and API never mark a task read.
- [ ] AC3: Each device independently persists Work, Quiet and Free and restores its own latest saved scene and brightness across takeover, idle, Quiet, Free and recoverable failure. Quiet uses the existing steady 10 percent policy and Work keeps its brightness policy. A change affecting one device does not clear the other device's effects, pending edits, mode or restoration state. Free makes no further device requests after a successful handoff. Display-cache clears, `setup --reset` and shared-source switching affect only the device they target, or say explicitly that they reset all devices.
- [ ] AC4: Keep two-second status epochs, the one outward pulse, red/yellow priority and one completion comet per eligible completion per device. Entering Work, registering a device, recovering a connection, switching layouts and editing project colors do not reset epochs or replay obsolete effects. New task-project overrides keep affected active comet sources until their existing completion boundary.
- [ ] AC5: Catch failures and schedule bounded retries per device. A failing device cannot abort the other device's due updates or overwrite its last successful outcome.
- [ ] AC6: CLI mode and status controls accept an explicit device target. With no target they address the original Lines device regardless of registry order. An unknown target is rejected rather than falling back to Lines.
- [ ] AC7: The protected controller, integration settings API and local MCP keep addressing the original Lines identity only. The shared wire contract, capability declaration, snapshots, credentials and request replay are unchanged. #64's power, brightness and saved-scene overrides and #28's hold on failed or uncertain machine requests apply to Lines only and never write to Panels. Registering Panels does not change what any existing credential can do.

### NL22 renderer

- [ ] AC8: Read supported NL22 layout data into stable one-zone triangle elements, keeping panel identities, coordinates, orientation and neighboring geometry. Exclude non-light modules. Reject malformed or unsupported geometry instead of mapping it as Lines. Use reported geometry; do not assign real panel IDs from the photo.
- [ ] AC9: Generate valid HTTP custom and static effect payloads for NL22. Lines-specific paired-zone assumptions stay in the Lines renderer. Both renderers run under the existing worker, with one writer per physical device and independently addressed transport.
- [ ] AC10: Whole triangles show the existing working green, question yellow, blocked red and unread blue states, with the two-second pulse, one outward status wave and completion comet. Travel is calculated within that device's arrangement. Overlapping effects keep red/yellow alert priority and active source reservations.
- [ ] AC11: One triangle supplies one task slot. Project reservations apply per triangle and support selecting a six-triangle region through ordinary multi-selection. title: Enroll a second Nanoleaf device on the Linux runtime

## Desired outcome

Provide a Linux command that adds NL22 Panels to the existing Lines installation without losing current state, and that starts the new device in Free so nothing lights up until the operator chooses.

Out of scope here: the retired Windows installation and its installer, backup and rollback tooling, WSL forwarding, firmware updates, hook migrations, remote ingress, and new services.

- [ ] AC1: An explicit enrollment command obtains or accepts a private NL22 credential, verifies the reported model and layout, and registers a stable device identity in the #41 registry without running fresh setup, clearing tasks, replacing trusted hooks, or altering the existing Lines identity.

Cached geometry and persisted preferences remain usable when a device is unavailable.

Use temporary Linux state directories containing Lines-only state and then two configured fake devices. title: Verify Lines and NL22 Panels together on the installed Linux runtime
body:
## Desired outcome

Confirm that Lines and original NL22 Light Panels display useful task status together on the existing Linux installation, operate independently, and restore their own scenes and brightness.

## Scope

One installation and everyday-use trial for one operator in Ubuntu WSL. Source prerequisites [#41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41), [#43](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/43), and [#45](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/45) are delivered. The wall map remains Lines-only; use the CLI `--device` target for Panels until [#44](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/44).

A later explicit installation task must authorize the intended devices, installation update, and bounded light sequence. Updating this issue does not authorize installation, pairing, or device operation.

Use the existing private Linux installation and [Linux installation guide](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/docs/linux-install.md). Never run fresh setup to update it. Updating installed source may require restarting affected processes; enrollment itself requires no service restart. No backup, upgrade, or rollback tooling is added here.

User-reported Panels hardware is NL22, firmware 5.2.2, hardware 1.6.2, with 18 triangles arranged as three connected hexagons and the middle hexagon raised. Treat this as an expectation to check against the device, not a source of panel identities. Obtain addresses and credentials from private configuration; keep the original photo private.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1 — Identify the trial: record the delivered source revision, confirm both intended device identities, and read the NL22 model, firmware, and layout. Check the expected triangle count and plausible physical arrangement using reported geometry and representative visible placement. Resolve a material mismatch before dependent tests; do not guess panel identities or change firmware.
- [x] AC2 — Update and enroll: update the existing Linux installation without fresh setup and enroll Panels in Free using the delivered command. Confirm existing Lines tasks, reservations and preferences remain available and normal task display through the existing input source still works. Keep the selected shared-monitoring source; do not switch back to legacy hooks for this trial. Preserve credentials and trusted hooks. Restart only processes needed for the source update; enrollment alone needs no restart.
- [x] AC3 — Check task display: use representative tasks and the existing synthetic effect previews to confirm a task appears once on each device, representative triangle placement makes sense, and shared completion/read evidence clears the corresponding indications on both. Observe working green, question yellow, blocked red, unread blue, a status pulse, an outward wave, and a completion effect. Confirm red/yellow alerts remain visible and Lines retain split-half behavior. This is a visual functional check, not precise timing or exhaustive transition testing. Do not mark Codex tasks read through the map or by editing Codex state.
- [x] AC4 — Check modes and restoration: briefly exercise Work, Quiet, and Free on each device. Confirm Quiet is steady at its intended brightness, changing one device's mode leaves the other alone, and each device restores its own saved scene and brightness at the agreed idle or Free boundary. Use targeted CLI commands for Panels; a full matrix of mixed-mode combinations is unnecessary.
- [x] AC5 — Check the existing map: confirm the wall map opens, still shows Lines, and one targeted Lines control works with Panels enrolled. Panels selection and triangle reservations remain outside this trial; the map selector follows in #44.
- [x] AC6 — Finish and record: keep the installed worker as the only light writer for each device throughout the trial. Restore the user-selected modes and scene preferences at the end. Record a concise result with the source revision, installation outcome, visible observations, scene restoration, final modes, and remaining problems. Separate transport acknowledgments from the user's visible-light confirmation. Exclude credentials, private addresses and paths, raw task/device data, and the original photo. Close only when the retained criteria pass and the user confirms the visible result; otherwise keep the issue open with the specific next action.

## Verification approach

Reuse source-test evidence from #41, #43, and #45. Perform the separately authorized installation and one bounded visual sequence, using synthetic tasks where possible, plus a normal task check through the installed shared-monitoring source. No new test harness, soak period, or production qualification exercise is required.

title: Combine Lines and Light Panels into one layout and allocation pool
body:
## Desired outcome

Eventually present Lines and Light Panels as one spatial layout and allocate each task once across a shared pool of their elements, replacing mirrored placement when that combined pool is selected.

## Scope

Record the future direction requested alongside the first mirrored-device release. Reuse stable device and element identity, one shared task owner, and the existing worker as the only light writer from [#41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41) and [#43](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/43). #41 keys placement by device and adds no separate pool identity; this design decides whether a pool column is needed. The verified mirrored configuration remains available as a baseline.

This issue is deferred design work. Do not enable a combined pool, redistribute tasks, invent placement rules, or mark it ready as part of the initial NL22 delivery. The user has chosen the eventual outcome; the behavior below still requires a focused design discussion.

## Decisions required before implementation readiness

- Decide how the two physical arrangements appear in one canvas, including their relative position, scale, orientation, and whether placements represent physical distance or a chosen logical arrangement.
- Decide allocation priority, project reservations, Shared overflow, capacity reporting, and element selection across one-zone triangles and two-zone Lines. Define what one task placement means without duplicating that task across the combined pool.
- Decide eligibility when devices have independent Work, Quiet, and Free modes or are unavailable, including whether and when tasks can move, and how existing reservations and active comet sources are preserved.
- Decide whether waves and comets stay within a device or cross the combined layout, and specify the timing and failure behavior without assuming synchronized transport or exact optical parity.
- Define opt-in migration from mirrored assignments that preserves tasks, unread evidence, preferences, and effect epochs, and whether a way back to mirrored placement is worth building for one operator. Identify any required API or renderer changes using the existing shared ownership boundaries.

## Acceptance criteria for the design phase

- [ ] AC1: After [#46](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/46), resolve the decisions above with the user and record observable allocation, layout, mixed-mode, outage, animation, and migration scenarios.
- [ ] AC2: The accepted design provides one task placement across the selected combined pool while keeping physical device identity and device ownership explicit. It does not duplicate provider interpretation or introduce a second writer.
- [ ] AC3: Assign settled requirements, lasting decisions, and delivery scope to the repository's existing specification, ADR, and GitHub owners. Define implementation issue boundaries and dependencies rather than silently expanding the completed initial release.
- [ ] AC4: Specify deterministic allocation and migration tests, browser cases and human UI approval, and separately authorized physical verification for any changed device behavior. Exact synchronization claims need their own evidence consistent with #15 and #17.
- [ ] AC5: Keep status:backlog and deferred until the required decisions and prerequisites are settled. Do not treat the first mirrored release or this ticket's existence as acceptance of a combined-pool implementation.

## Verification approach

The initial deliverable is a reviewed, decision-complete design with testable examples covering the decisions above. No source tests, UI candidates, or device operations are claimed by this backlog definition. Later implementation must follow the repository's normal source, UI, installation, and physical evidence gates.

## Dependencies

- Blocked by [#46](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/46) and unresolved design choices. The first release must establish verified independent control before combined-pool migration is designed for delivery.
- Reuse foundations from [#41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41) and [#43](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/43); coordinate with #15 and #17 when defining renderer and timing implications. Shared monitoring and MCP infrastructure remain with their existing issues.

## Delivery target

Deferred planning and design only at this stage. Implementation, combined-pool activation, and hardware changes require a separately accepted follow-on plan. This issue must not be marked ready now.

## Planning and delivery

Any later accepted source implementation follows AGENTS.md and docs/sdlc.md: an isolated issue branch, issue-linked OpenSpec planning, focused red/green checks, independent Standards and Specification reviews against the same committed comparison, required CI, guarded merge, and main-CI readback. UI changes require human approval of the current candidate.

## Revision note

I replaced "one Windows writer" with the existing worker, noted that #41 no longer carries a separate pool identity so this design owns that decision, made the reversible-return question explicit rather than required, and removed the publication boilerplate. The edit history holds the prior text.

title: Expose connector geometry for the Prism wall map
body:
## Desired outcome

The wall map can place crystal tubes against the flat faces of the actual hexagonal connectors, using validated layout data and the existing physical Line identities.

## Scope

Extend the existing geometry cache and wall-state projection with a small, versioned connector and Line-end contract. This is the geometry prerequisite for the approved Prism UI integration.

At planning baseline `ea3b95661352f927aceaf92b62d74660978c201f`, `bridge/wall_server.py:ensure_geometry` retains only shapeType 18 zone positions and skips refresh when that cache exists. `project_map.geometry` exposes three points per Line, not exact connector centers. A raw-layout fixture alone therefore does not establish that an existing cache supplies the required information.

Preserve connector centers, source identities, endpoint relationships, and orientation through the existing backend owner. Keep `line_groups` order, `project_map.line_id`, physical numbering, and the two zone IDs in their current order. Define where orientation, Y inversion, rotation, and flips apply so each transform runs once.

This work covers current Lines with six-face hexagonal connectors. It does not add Light Panels, 90-degree connectors, multi-device allocation, a second state owner, a new controller API, or light writes. It does not migrate Windows installation data. The separately planned fresh Linux installation reuses this wall server and UI; coordinate overlapping geometry/cache changes without making that service move a prerequisite.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] AC1: A credential-free, versioned geometry projection identifies connector centers, the connector at each Line end, stable Line IDs/numbers, and ordered zone IDs. Duplicate controller entries at one housing retain source identity without rendering duplicate housings. Existing wall-state fields and callers continue working.
- [x] AC2: A fresh layout and an existing zone-only cache both obtain connector geometry through the designated backend path. Enrichment preserves existing tasks, reservations, preferences, assignments, scenes, and epochs. It requires no fresh setup, Windows process launch, browser device request, or additional light writer.
- [x] AC3: Invalid, incomplete, unsupported, or unavailable layout data cannot replace the last valid geometry or fabricate a connection. With no exact connector data, the existing wall remains usable through a documented fallback and bounded retry. Concurrent readers cannot observe a partially replaced cache. Geometry reads do not create continuous device polling in Free mode or requests tied to animation frames.
- [x] AC4: The saved 15-Line layout and synthetic chain, branch, cycle, and disconnected fixtures preserve topology, relative lengths, Line identity, and zone ownership across global orientation, map rotations, and flips. Where two controller IDs describe one connector housing, they resolve consistently. The renderer can derive flat-face joins without rounding visible Line endpoints into guessed connector centers.
- [x] AC5: The new geometry fields contain only the data needed for drawing. They exclude tokens, device addresses, configuration objects, local paths, and task metadata. Existing Host, origin, authentication, and response restrictions remain effective; this issue does not widen the protected machine API.
- [x] AC6: Document the geometry contract, compatibility behavior, cache owner, and transform convention for the renderer. Link issue-specific OpenSpec scenarios to these criteria. Reconcile with any intervening device-geometry or Linux-runtime changes before selecting the final schema.

## Verification approach

All checks below are planned, not executed by issue publication.

| Criteria | Planned evidence |
| --- | --- |
| AC1, AC4 | Isolated producer/consumer fixtures asserting exact IDs, numbering, zone order, connector centers, transforms, and topology; browser smoke check against the existing map. |
| AC2, AC3 | Fresh and legacy cache fixtures, repeated enrichment, simultaneous reads, malformed/missing connector entries, timeout/failure and recovery. Snapshot application state before/after and count fake device calls, including repeated Free-mode reads. |
| AC5 | Privacy canaries in backend-only configuration and metadata; assert absence from the new projection. Exercise rejected Host/origin requests and existing protected-write tests. |
| AC6 | Contract/specification review against current main and the accepted renderer inputs. |

Run `python3 scripts/check.py` and `npm run test:browser` for the API change. After applicable OpenSpec changes and `npm ci`, run `npm run check:workflow` and `npm run test:workflow`. Use synthetic state and fake lights. These checks do not establish installation or physical-light acceptance.

## Dependencies and scope references

- No unfinished feature prerequisite. Ready for separately authorized source delivery.
- Preserve [Line identification](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/openspec/specs/wall-line-identification/spec.md) and the [bridge behavior contract](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/blob/main/bridge/README.md).
- Coordinate schema changes with [device-aware geometry #41](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/41); it is related work, not a required multi-device implementation.
- Exact physical-frame mirroring remains [#15](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/15) and [#17](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/17). Shared-frontend configuration remains [#49](https://github.com/jimmie-potts/codex-nanoleaf/issues/49).

## Assessment

Planning, 2026-09-09, source baseline above.

- Complexity: medium. Cache acquisition, validation, transforms, and the browser projection must agree while retaining existing callers.
- Uncertainty: medium. The bounded investigation is to derive endpoint relationships and shared housings from sanitized controller fixtures, then prove an additive contract against old and new caches before renderer integration. Unsupported geometry must produce an explicit fallback.
- Impact: high. The geometry response is derived from credential-bearing configuration and cache writes share a boundary with application preferences. Privacy and preservation checks are required even though the intended feature is visual.
- Readiness: ready. Product decisions are settled; the bounded contract investigation is part of this item. Reassess if #41 or the Linux move changes ownership/schema, or fixtures cannot establish endpoint relationships.

## Delivery target and handoff

Source-only. Publication starts no implementation, installation, service, hook, or device operation.

Future delivery uses the current SDLC, an owned isolated worktree, the exact issue-linked OpenSpec change, and independent Standards and Specification reviews of the same committed candidate.
